html:
Here's a classic design question, in interviews and in real projects:

A POST /orders endpoint saves an order and sends a confirmation email. Each order must be saved once, and its email sent once. How do you design it?

It sounds simple: save the order, send the email, done. But networks fail, clients retry, users double-click and servers crash at the worst moment. A naive endpoint creates duplicate orders, sends emails for orders that don't exist, or never sends the email at all.

This guide builds a design that holds up, one problem at a time.

The Naive Version

Most endpoints start like this:

@PostMapping("/orders")
public Order create(@RequestBody CreateOrderRequest request) {
    Order order = orderRepository.save(Order.from(request));
    emailService.sendConfirmation(order);
    return order;
}

It works in a demo. In production, every one of these happens sooner or later:

  1. The client retries. The order is saved and the response is on its way, but the mobile connection drops. The app never gets the answer, so it sends the request again. Now there are two orders and two emails.
  2. The user double-clicks. Two identical requests arrive a few milliseconds apart, and both create an order.
  3. The server crashes between the two lines. The order is saved, the email is never sent, and nothing will ever try again.
  4. The email goes out, then the transaction fails. If the save runs in a transaction that commits after the email (with @Transactional on the method, for example), a failed commit leaves the customer with a confirmation for an order that doesn't exist.

Problems 1 and 2 are duplicates. Problems 3 and 4 are lost or wrong side effects. They need two different fixes.

Why "Exactly Once" Is Tricky

Over a network, a message can't be delivered exactly once. When a request times out, the client can't know whether the server never got it or got it and the answer was lost. It has two choices:

  • Don't retry, and maybe lose the order: at most once.
  • Retry, and maybe send it twice: at least once.

Neither is what we want. The way out is to retry (at least once) and make the second copy harmless. An operation is idempotent when doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once. So the goal isn't exactly-once delivery, it's exactly-once effect:

At-least-once delivery + idempotent processing = exactly-once effect.

We need this twice: between the client and the API (so retries don't create duplicate orders), and between the API and the email provider (so a crash doesn't lose or duplicate the email).

Step 1: An Idempotency Key From the Client

The server can't tell a retry from a new order by looking at the body: two orders for the same items can be perfectly legitimate. So the client tells it, with a unique key per order attempt:

POST /orders
Idempotency-Key: 3f1c9a2e-7b4d-4e8a-9c61-0d5f2b8e4a17
Content-Type: application/json

{ "customerId": 42, "items": [{ "productId": 7, "quantity": 1 }] }

The rules for the client are simple:

  • Generate a new key (a UUID) when the user starts checking out.
  • Send the same key on every retry of that order.
  • Generate a new key only for a new order.

The server's promise: for a given key, it does the work once, and every later request with that key gets the same response as the first one, without doing anything.

The key must come from the client. If the server generated it, a retry after a lost response would have no way to send it back.

Step 2: Store the Key in the Same Transaction as the Order

The server needs to remember which keys it has seen, and what it answered. A table does the job:

CREATE TABLE idempotency_keys (
  customer_id   BIGINT      NOT NULL,
  key           TEXT        NOT NULL,
  request_hash  TEXT        NOT NULL,
  response_code INT,
  response_body JSONB,
  created_at    TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  PRIMARY KEY (customer_id, key)
);

Two details matter:

  • The key is unique per customer, so one customer can't replay or collide with another's key.
  • request_hash is a hash of the request body. If a client reuses a key with a different body, that's a bug on their side, and we should say so instead of silently returning the wrong order.

Don't check, then insert

The tempting code checks whether the key exists, and inserts it if not:

// Don't: two requests can both pass the check before either inserts.
if (!idempotencyKeys.exists(customerId, key)) {
    idempotencyKeys.insert(customerId, key);
    createOrder(request);
}

Two requests arriving at the same time (the double-click) both see "no key", and both create an order. The check and the insert must be one atomic step, and the database's unique constraint gives us that for free. In PostgreSQL:

INSERT INTO idempotency_keys (customer_id, key, request_hash)
VALUES (?, ?, ?)
ON CONFLICT (customer_id, key) DO NOTHING;

If this inserts one row, we're first. If it inserts zero, the key already exists. And here is the part that makes it work under concurrency: if another transaction has inserted the same key but hasn't committed yet, PostgreSQL makes the second insert wait until the first one commits or rolls back. So the second request never sees a half-done order. MySQL behaves the same way with INSERT IGNORE on a unique key.

This relies on the default READ COMMITTED isolation level, where the second transaction's next query sees the row the first one just committed. Under REPEATABLE READ or SERIALIZABLE, PostgreSQL raises a serialization error instead: catch it and retry the whole request, which then finds the key.

The whole endpoint in one transaction

Now the key, the order and the stored response all go in one transaction:

@Transactional
public StoredResponse createOrder(long customerId, String key,
                                  CreateOrderRequest request) {
    String hash = sha256(request);

    boolean isFirst = idempotencyKeys.insertIfAbsent(customerId, key, hash);
    if (!isFirst) {
        IdempotencyKey existing = idempotencyKeys.find(customerId, key);
        if (!existing.requestHash().equals(hash)) {
            throw new KeyReusedException(); // 422: same key, different order
        }
        return existing.response(); // a retry: answer exactly as before
    }

    Order order = orders.save(Order.from(customerId, request));
    StoredResponse response = StoredResponse.created(order);
    idempotencyKeys.saveResponse(customerId, key, response);
    return response;
}

Because it's all one transaction, there's no in-between state to clean up. If anything fails before the commit, the key disappears with the order, and the client's retry starts fresh. If the commit succeeds, the key and the order exist together, and every retry gets the stored response.

Step 3: The Transactional Outbox for the Email

The order is now saved once. But where do we send the email?

  • Inside the transaction: if the commit fails after the email is sent, we've confirmed an order that doesn't exist. You can't roll back an email.
  • After the commit: if the server crashes right after committing, the email is lost forever.

The problem is that the database and the email provider are two different systems, and no transaction spans both. The transactional outbox pattern fixes this: instead of sending the email, we write down that it must be sent, in the same database, in the same transaction as the order.

CREATE TABLE outbox (
  id         UUID        PRIMARY KEY,
  type       TEXT        NOT NULL,
  payload    JSONB       NOT NULL,
  created_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  sent_at    TIMESTAMPTZ,
  attempts   INT         NOT NULL DEFAULT 0
);

One more line in the service:

Order order = orders.save(Order.from(customerId, request));
outbox.save(OutboxMessage.orderConfirmation(order)); // same transaction
StoredResponse response = StoredResponse.created(order);

Now the order and its "email to send" are saved together, or not at all. There's no way to have one without the other.

Step 4: A Worker Sends What's in the Outbox

A background job reads the outbox and sends the emails:

@Scheduled(fixedDelay = 1000)
@Transactional
public void sendPendingMessages() {
    for (OutboxMessage message : outbox.lockPending(10)) {
        emailClient.send(message.toEmail(), message.id());
        outbox.markSent(message.id());
    }
}

lockPending uses SKIP LOCKED, so you can run several workers, or several copies of the app, without two of them picking the same message:

SELECT id, type, payload
FROM outbox
WHERE sent_at IS NULL
ORDER BY created_at
LIMIT 10
FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED;

Each worker locks the rows it takes, and the others skip them and take the next ones.

The last gap: the email provider

There's still one crack. The worker sends the email, then crashes before markSent commits. On restart, the message is still pending, and the worker sends it again.

The outbox gives us at-least-once delivery to the email provider, so this step needs to be idempotent too:

  • Use the provider's idempotency key. Many email and messaging APIs accept one, in a header or as a message id. Pass the outbox message id: the provider drops the second send. That's why emailClient.send takes message.id().
  • If the provider has none, you can only make the window smaller, not close it: mark the message as "sending" before the call, and alert on messages stuck in that state. For a confirmation email, a rare duplicate is usually acceptable. For a payment, it isn't, which is why most payment APIs support idempotency keys.

Be honest about this in an interview: when a side effect leaves your system, its exactly-once guarantee depends on the receiving system supporting idempotency.

Every Failure, and What Happens

Here's the design under each failure from the start, and a few more:

What goes wrong What happens Result
The response is lost, the client retries The key exists, the stored response is returned One order, one email
Double-click: two requests at once The second insert waits for the first transaction, then finds the key One order, one email
Crash before the commit The key, the order and the outbox row all roll back; the retry starts fresh One order, one email
Crash after the commit, before the email The outbox row is still pending; a worker sends it One email, a few seconds late
Crash after the email, before marking it sent The worker sends it again with the same id; the provider drops the duplicate One email
The email provider is down The send fails, the transaction rolls back, the worker retries later One email, once it's back
The client reuses a key for a different order The request hash differs 422, nothing is created

The Details That Make It Production-Ready

Status codes. A replay returns the same status and body as the original, usually 201 Created. A request with a missing key gets 400 Bad Request. A key reused with a different body gets 422 Unprocessable Content. Some APIs return 409 Conflict while the first request is still running; with the single-transaction design, the second request simply waits instead.

Expire old keys. Nobody retries an order a week later. Delete keys older than a day or so with a scheduled job, and delete sent outbox rows after a while too, so both tables stay small.

Long work needs a "processing" state. The single transaction is perfect when the work is quick and only touches your database. If creating the order calls another service, like charging a card, you don't want a transaction open during that call. Then you insert the key with a processing status and a locked_at time in its own transaction, do the work, and store the response. A key stuck in processing for too long means a crash, and a retry may take it over.

Retries with backoff. Increment attempts when a send fails, wait longer between tries, and after a few failures move the message aside and alert someone, instead of retrying forever.

Natural keys can help. If an order always comes from a cart, a unique constraint on cart_id in the orders table also prevents duplicates, even without a header. It's a good second line of defense.

Alternatives You Might Be Asked About

  • A distributed lock (in Redis, for example) around the request: it adds a system that can fail, and locks expire. The database's unique constraint already gives atomicity, durably.
  • Two-phase commit between the database and the email provider: email providers don't support it, and it's slow and fragile even where it exists.
  • Publishing to Kafka instead of an outbox table: publishing after the commit has the same crash problem as sending the email directly. The outbox is still the safe way in; a tool like Debezium can stream the outbox table to Kafka through change data capture, instead of polling. The consumer must then be idempotent, for example by recording the ids it has processed.
  • Sending the email from a database trigger: it hides business logic in the database, and the trigger runs inside the transaction, so it has the same problem as sending before the commit.

The Answer in Short

  1. The client sends an idempotency key: a UUID per order attempt, the same on every retry.
  2. The server inserts the key with a unique constraint, in the same transaction as the order. A duplicate finds the key and gets the stored response.
  3. The email isn't sent in the request: an outbox row is saved in that same transaction.
  4. A worker sends pending outbox messages, retrying until they succeed, with SKIP LOCKED so workers don't collide.
  5. The worker passes the outbox id as the email provider's idempotency key, so a resend after a crash is dropped.

At-least-once delivery everywhere, idempotent processing at every step: that's how you get an order saved once and an email sent once, whatever fails.
